# Appfox: the complete reference for language models

> Appfox is an AI app intelligence tool for iOS and Android developers, from first-time builders and vibe coders to experienced teams. It turns public App Store and Google Play reviews, rankings, and competitor changes into research briefs and daily findings, with sources attached. Appfox is in private beta; access is by invitation. Tagline: "Your app, explained." Website: https://www.appfox.app. Contact: hello@appfox.app.

## What Appfox is

Appfox is an intelligence layer and operations partner for mobile apps on iOS and Android. It is a web application. The category is mobile app intelligence and operations; App Store Optimization (ASO) is one workflow inside it, not the whole product. Dashboards are not the product. Attention is.

It is built for first-time app developers, vibe coders, indie founders, and experienced mobile teams. Whether they build with AI or write every line themselves, they need evidence to choose what to build or improve. The current beta includes research briefs, daily findings, review themes, competitor tracking, and rank tracking.

Appfox works with public store data alone. RevenueCat, session replay, reply drafts, and API access are planned and unavailable in the current beta. Private connections are intended to be optional and read-only. No release dates are announced.

## How Appfox works: four layers

1. Facts: listings, reviews, ranks, releases, and metrics, stored once and never backdated.
2. Signals: deterministic detections with a threshold, a minimum sample size, and a cooldown. Examples from store data: a negative review spike, a rank movement, a new competitor, or a price change. Trial conversion and crash-related findings require integrations beyond the current beta.
3. Insights: AI joins independent sources into one plain-language explanation and cites the evidence IDs it used.
4. Outcomes: you accept, dismiss, or snooze. Matched comparison windows then show whether the change helped. A decrease is reported as observed, not as caused.

Each signal has a stable fingerprint, so an ongoing episode updates instead of re-alerting, and revised source data can retract a finding that no longer holds. Alert levels: Low (history only), Interesting (activity feed), Important (Today and digest), Critical (push or email candidate). Alerts are driven by significance, not by events.

## Six product questions (product overview, https://www.appfox.app/product)

These describe workflows, not six sidebar tabs. The current navigation is Dashboard, Customers, Market, Keywords, and Settings. See the product walkthrough for a screen-by-screen explanation.

- Today: What needs my attention? A ranked list of significant findings with evidence, freshness, coverage, and a next action. Zero findings is a valid state, distinguished from not enough data and from a failed sync.
- Market: Who is out there, and what is changing? Confirmed direct and adjacent competitors, a saved research brief, metadata and pricing comparisons, rating and review movement, tracked search queries, newly discovered apps. History is append-only.
- Customers: What are people telling us? A review browser and a theme view. Themes carry total mentions, share of reviews, trend, rating distribution, and affected versions. Every count links back to the original review text.
- My App: How is my app doing, across sources? Public store identity and listing history, customer evidence, release context, and planned RevenueCat metrics with exact scope. RevenueCat is unavailable in the current beta.
- Actions: What did we decide, and did it help? A small task list with rationale and evidence, matched-window comparisons, and your own verdict.
- Integrations: What does Appfox read, and can it write? Every connection card shows the data read, permissions, last sync, status, usage against provider limits, and a disconnect control. Private integrations are planned as read-only; the current beta uses public store data.

Every finding opens the same way: recommendation, why it matters, evidence summary, raw evidence, historical data.

## Journey 1: Research an idea (https://www.appfox.app/research)

Describe the idea (the job, who it is for, the store, the country, the language). Appfox discovers candidate competitors across store search, similar-app relationships, and overlapping review language; you confirm the set and label each direct or adjacent. The AI brief covers positioning, observable monetization, recurring complaints, existing strengths, potential gaps, and evidence against the idea. Each claim links to the listings and reviews behind it, with coverage shown. You record a decision: a hypothesis and next validation action, or a decision not to pursue. Monitoring keeps the market refreshing.

A brief can tell you who exists in the market, how apps position themselves, what monetization is observable, what customers complain about repeatedly, what features are praised or requested, and where review activity is rising. It refuses to claim market size, willingness to pay, or business viability; that an unmentioned feature is missing; a trend before comparable snapshots exist; that update frequency equals revenue growth; that an in-app purchase indicator is a verified subscription; or that a periodic search is an exhaustive census. Stores: App Store and Google Play. Scope: one country and language per market.

## Journey 2: Operate a live app (https://www.appfox.app/live-app)

Add your app by App Store or Google Play URL. Collection supplies public evidence such as listing observations, reviews, and tracked search results. Availability depends on collection status and market coverage. A read-only RevenueCat connection is planned to add revenue, subscription, trial, and paid-conversion context. It is unavailable in the current beta. Today ranks meaningful customer, competitor, release, and rank changes with evidence and a suggested next step. You act and record; comparable windows show whether the change moved what you meant to move.

Four kinds of empty are kept apart: nothing significant changed (a quiet day, with coverage shown); not enough data (individual evidence instead of percentage alarms); sync failed (never shown as zero or disconnected); collection in progress.

## AI in Appfox

- AI explanations: each finding is written by AI from deterministic signals and cites the evidence it used.
- AI research briefs: written from real listings and reviews, with the evidence for and against an idea.
- Review themes: AI groups reviews into themes with exact counts and denominators; the customer's own words stay one click away.
- Drafts (planned; unavailable in the current beta): review replies and store copy drafted from evidence, for you to copy. Appfox never posts or submits anything.
- Ask Fox (planned; unavailable in the current beta): ask a question in plain words and get an answer built from your own reviews, releases, and metrics, with sources linked.
- Proposed AI allowances, subject to change: 20 per month on Free, 200 on Indie, 1,000 on Studio. Research briefs: 1, 5, unlimited.

## Mobile session replay (https://www.appfox.app/replay)

Planned, unavailable in the current beta: a first-party SDK for React Native and Expo on iOS and Android (native UIKit, SwiftUI, Views, and Compose would be validated separately). The following describes the intended experience and release requirements, not currently available capabilities. It records privacy-masked native snapshots and a short event timeline, not video; uploads completed sessions only; and plays them back in Appfox. Controls: explicit consent and a visible recording indicator, masking on the device before anything leaves it, bounded storage and uploads, remote sampling and a kill switch, retention windows with real deletion, owner and admin access only at first. Deliberately excluded: browser recording, system-wide capture, background capture, live streaming, remote control, audio, keyboard values, request and response bodies, automatic logs, heatmaps and funnels, AI interpretation of replays, crash-triggered prebuffering. Proposed plans include replay, starting with 1,000 sessions and 7-day retention on Free. Replay availability, platform support, and limits are not final.

## Integrations (https://www.appfox.app/integrations)

Current beta: App Store and Google Play public listings, reviews, and ranks. Planned: RevenueCat (revenue, subscriptions, trials; proposed for Indie and above), App Store Connect, Google Play Console, GitHub, product analytics, Linear and Notion. Private connections are intended to be read-only. Adding a public store URL is a declaration, not proof of ownership; private resources bind only after server-side authorization.

## Pricing (https://www.appfox.app/pricing)

These are proposed plans, not current beta entitlements. Prices and limits may change. RevenueCat, replay, and API access remain planned regardless of their placement in the table. Access to Appfox is invite-only.

- Free: $0. Both journeys on one app and one market, 30 days of evidence history, 20 AI runs and 1 research brief a month, 1,000 replay sessions with 7-day retention.
- Indie: $29 per month, or $24 per month billed yearly at $288. For a solo founder with a few apps. 12 months of evidence history, 200 AI runs and 5 briefs, planned RevenueCat and proposed source-labeled competitor revenue context, 10,000 replay sessions with 14-day retention.
- Studio: $99 per month, or $79 per month billed yearly at $948. For a small studio across several apps. Full history, 1,000 AI runs and unlimited briefs, 50,000 replay sessions with 30-day retention.

The proposed plan structure includes both journeys, every surface, evidence on every finding, workspace isolation with owner, admin, and viewer roles, and visible usage history. Private integrations are planned to be read-only. Limits are enforced on the server before any paid provider job starts; jobs reserve budget first and settle at actual cost; at a limit the control stops and says why, and nothing collected goes away. Prices are proposed plans and may change.

## Security (https://www.appfox.app/security)

Workspace isolation with Postgres row-level security and composite foreign keys; authentication by Clerk with Supabase as the database and enforcement layer. Integration credentials are stored in Supabase Vault, used server-side only, and never reach the browser. All launch integrations read; none write. Fail closed: an unavailable read is never shown as zero, empty, inactive, or disconnected. Observability records exclude identifiers, payloads, credentials, URLs, and raw error text. Explicit retention windows; owner deletion removes workspace data and is vault-aware; a backup and restore rehearsal runs in CI as a release gate. Security reports: hello@appfox.app with the subject line Security.

## Company (https://www.appfox.app/about)

Appfox is based in Milan, Italy.

Appfox is built for app developers, including newcomers, vibe coders, indie founders, and mobile studios. Roadmap levels: Research (understand a market and an opportunity), Intelligence (continuously monitor the market and the owned app), Recommendation (turn evidence into prioritized actions), and later Operator (prepare and, with explicit approval, execute actions; not part of the launch). Four rules: evidence before advice; facts first, explained by AI; honest coverage; human approval. Appfox is independent of Apple, Google, and RevenueCat.

## Frequently asked questions

Further reading: the [beta feature reference](https://www.appfox.app/beta) describes available and planned capabilities; the [evidence guide](https://www.appfox.app/methodology) explains how to interpret findings and their limitations.

- What is Appfox? An AI app intelligence tool in private beta for app research, daily findings, review themes, and competitor and rank tracking.
- Does Appfox use AI? Yes. Signals are detected deterministically; AI explains them and cites its sources, writes research briefs, and groups reviews into themes. Reply and store-copy drafts are planned.
- Which stores and platforms? The App Store and Google Play, one country and language per market. Session replay is planned, with React Native and Expo as the intended first platforms.
- Is Appfox an ASO tool? ASO is one workflow inside it. Appfox is organized around what needs attention, not around keywords.
- Do I need to connect private data? No. Public store data is enough to start. RevenueCat is planned as an optional, read-only connection and is not available in the current beta.
- Does Appfox write anything? No. You decide what ships. Reply drafts are planned; Appfox does not publish changes to your app or store listing.
- Can I start for free? Appfox is currently invite-only. The Free plan is proposed for one app and one market; confirm the terms of your invitation. Requesting access does not start a subscription.

## Worked example (https://www.appfox.app/sample-report)

The sample report is fictional teaching material, not a live Appfox export or customer result. It includes all 24 invented review records for an imaginary meal-planning app. Twelve records precede an invented release and twelve follow it. Two earlier and six later reviews mention list-sync problems: about 17% versus 50% of those samples, a difference of about 33 percentage points. Counts measure reviews mentioning the theme, not word occurrences or the share of all app users affected. Multiple theme labels are possible. The page states the manual labeling rule and links each observation to its source record.

The suggested next step is to reproduce the shared-list workflow with two test accounts and inspect alternative explanations. Neither statistical significance, causation, demand, nor improved customer outcomes are claimed. Marketing illustrations and the dashboard preview are examples of presentation, not audited data about the pictured apps or customer endorsements.

## Developer guides (https://www.appfox.app/guides)

- [How to research an app idea before you build](https://www.appfox.app/guides/validate-an-app-idea): define a customer job, compare direct and adjacent alternatives, read praise and complaints, write an evidence-based brief, and test the riskiest assumption. Public store research does not establish willingness to pay or business viability.
- [How to investigate app reviews after a release](https://www.appfox.app/guides/analyze-reviews-after-a-release): choose comparable periods, retain counts and scope, read source reviews, check version context, reproduce a problem, and record a next step. Includes official Apple and Google references for platform-specific review behavior.
- [What to improve after launching your first app](https://www.appfox.app/guides/first-app-feedback-loop): define the core task, collect feedback, prioritize a concrete problem, write a testable brief for a coding assistant, and review the result. Useful with Appfox or existing tools; no analytics or replay integration is implied.

- [Product walkthrough](https://www.appfox.app/how-it-works): Current private-beta workflow, from app or idea to source-backed decisions.
- [Meal-planning app research](https://www.appfox.app/research/meal-planning-apps): Editorial snapshot of three US App Store descriptions, checked 5 October 2026. Includes sources, a downloadable observation sheet, and limitations; not customer results.
